content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses identify lamp oil primarily as the Holy Spirit — His indwelling presence, empowering grace, and illumination that fuels the believer's light — grounded chiefly in Zechariah 4, Matthew 25:1-13, and the tabernacle lamp texts (Exodus 27:20-21), with anointing passages (1 Sam 16:13; Acts 10:38) as reinforcement. Alternatives listed include readiness/watchfulness, genuine faith or grace, good works/charity (patristic), the Word of God, and non-transferable personal obedience/testimony (LDS). Two responses claim settled consensus; two note the identification is dominant popularly but contested exegetically.","book_summary":"The book defines lamp oil as 'the tested, pressed fruit of the Spirit, stored as evidence of faithful obedience and burned to give a visible example that lights the Way' — i.e., not the Spirit Himself but the product the Spirit produces in the believer: obedience to commandments, tested character, and visible good works that serve as light to others. Its citations foreground commandment-keeping and the word hidden in the heart (Ps 119; Prov 6:23; 7:1-3; Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:27; 1 John 2:4) and good works shining before men (Matt 5:16). The book explicitly flags the common teaching ('the Holy Spirit — anointing, consecration, and empowering') as the view it departs from.","consensus_core_identification":"Lamp oil = the Holy Spirit (His presence, empowering, and sustaining grace within the believer).","book_core_identification":"Lamp oil = the pressed, stored fruit of the Spirit — faithful obedience and tested works produced in the believer — burned as visible testimony, distinct from the Spirit who produces it.","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book applies the symbol to the same key texts (Ex 27:20; Zech 4; Matt 25) but reclassifies what the oil is in them: where consensus reads the Spirit as the fuel, the book reads the believer's Spirit-produced obedience and works. It adds texts consensus does not use for oil (Ps 141:5; Prov 21:20; 23:23; 27:5-9; Ps 119) and reads Matt 25:9's 'buy for yourselves' through Prov 23:23 ('buy the truth'), making the oil something acquired through obedience rather than a divine person received.","material_contradiction":"The Spirit (divine source) and the fruit of the Spirit (human product of obedience, stored as evidence) are different referents; oil cannot be both the Holy Spirit Himself and the tested obedience the Spirit produces, in the same context and sense. The book's common-view note signals it consciously rejects the Spirit identification as the primary meaning.","rationale":"The consensus core is a clear, unanimous identification of lamp oil with the Holy Spirit. The book replaces that referent with the Spirit's product — obedience, tested works, testimony — keeping only a causal connection ('fruit of the Spirit'). A source and its product remain different referents, especially where the book expressly frames the Spirit reading as merely 'commonly taught.' Although the book's reading resembles listed alternatives (good works, non-transferable obedience/testimony), the classification measures the book against the consensus's central identification, which the book rejects and replaces rather than narrows. Hence DIVERGENT with core CONTRADICTS and extension PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION (same biblical cases, different referent, plus added commandment texts).","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"The book's identification is arguably covered by the blind alternatives — good works (patristic), and Response A's LDS-style 'individually acquired obedience and testimony that cannot be borrowed' — so one could argue the relationship is closer to an elevation of a listed minority view than a wholly divergent replacement; additionally, Zech 4's 'not by might... but by my spirit' printed with the entry cuts against the book by explicitly tying the oil imagery to the Spirit rather than to human obedience.","confidence":"high"}
